# Week 13 - Statistical Modeling and Quarto

## Import Data

Import data from week 11 ecv_by_specimen.csv and print the dimensions and first five rows.

```{python}
#| label: setup

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import patsy
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from patsy.contrasts import Poly
from plotnine import *

# Locate the project root (the folder containing _quarto.yml) so the
# data path works whether we render from the project root, from week13,
# or run cells interactively in an IDE.
root = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]
            if (p / '_quarto.yml').exists())
path2ecv = root / 'part3_AL' / 'week11' / 'ecv_by_specimen.csv'
ecv = pd.read_csv(path2ecv)

# Grade is a ordered categorical variable. 
# We need to set the ordering or else it will default
# to alphabetical. 
grade_order = ['archaic', 'mega', 'trans', 'pre.mod']
ecv['grade'] = pd.Categorical(ecv['grade'], 
    categories=grade_order, 
    ordered=True)

print(ecv.shape)
ecv.head()
```

## Patsy

Patsy (https://patsy.readthedocs.io) is a Python library for describing statistical models using a compact formula language. If you have used R, the syntax will feel familiar because Patsy was directly inspired by R's formula interface.

### 2.1 Patsy Design Matrices

```{python}
#| label: design-matrix-simple
y, X = patsy.dmatrices('ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma', data=ecv, return_type='dataframe')
print('Response (y):')
print(y.head())
print('\nDesign matrix (X):')
print(X.head())
print('\nX columns:', X.columns.tolist())
```

### 2.2 Build a multiple design matrix

```{python}
#| label: design-matrix-multiple

y2, X2 = patsy.dmatrices('ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma + C(grade)', data=ecv, return_type='dataframe')
print('X2 shape:', X2.shape)
print('X2 columns:', X2.columns.tolist())
print(X2.head(8))
```

### 2.3 Inspect the encoding

Check which rows have a 1 in the `C(grade)[T.Homo_erectus]` column (or whichever dummy column appears for a grade you recognize)

```{python}
#| label: inspect-encoding

col = [c for c in X2.columns if 'T.' in c][0]
print(f'Rows where {col} == 1:')
print(ecv.loc[X2[col] == 1, ['taxon', 'grade', 'ecv_median_cm3', 'age_mid_Ma']].head())
```

### 2.4 Build a model with polynomial contrast

Categorical (dummy) coding asks: “How does each group differ from a baseline?”

One group is the reference; coefficients are deviations from it Makes no assumption about order Best when categories are nominal or when you want pairwise comparisons

Polynomial contrast coding asks: “What is the shape of the trend across the ordered sequence?”

No reference group; coefficients describe linear, quadratic, cubic trends Requires a meaningful order Best when categories have a natural progression and you expect a directional effect

For your evolutionary grades (archaic → mega → trans → pre.mod), polynomial coding is more appropriate because the order is theoretically meaningful and the scientifically interesting question is whether ECV increases monotonically across the sequence — not whether each grade differs from archaic specifically.

```{python}
#| label: design-matrix-multiple-poly

y3, X3 = patsy.dmatrices('ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma + C(grade, Poly())', data=ecv, return_type='dataframe')
print('X3 shape:', X3.shape)
print('X3 columns:', X3.columns.tolist())
print(X3.head(8))
```

## Part 3 OLS Regression

### 3.1 Simple regression: ECV \~ age

```{python}
#| label: ols-simple
model1 = smf.ols('ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma', data=ecv).fit()
print(model1.summary())
```

### 3.2 Multiple regression: ECV \~ age + grade

Add grade as a predictor variable.

```{python}
#| label: ols-multiple
model2 = smf.ols('ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma + C(grade)', data=ecv).fit()
print(model2.summary())
```

### 3.3 Residual diagnostic plot

A key OLS assumption is that residuals are randomly scattered around zero. Plot fitted values against residuals to check:

```{python}
#| label: fig-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals vs. fitted values for the multiple regression model"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

ecv_diag = ecv.copy()
ecv_diag['fitted'] = model2.fittedvalues
ecv_diag['resid'] = model2.resid

(
    ggplot(ecv_diag, aes(x='fitted', y='resid'))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.5)
    + geom_hline(yintercept=0, color='red', linetype='dashed')
    + labs(x='Fitted values', y='Residuals',
           title='Residuals vs. Fitted')
    + theme_bw()
)
```

### 3.4 Interaction term

Fit a model with an interaction between age and grade:

```{python}
#| label: ols-interaction

model3 = smf.ols('ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma * C(grade)', data=ecv).fit()
print(model3.summary())
```

## Part 4 Figures and Inline Results in Quarto

### 4.1 A polished figure with a cross-reference

Add a publication-quality figure showing observed ECV vs. age, with the fitted line from model1 overlaid:

```{python}
#| label: fig-ecv-fitted
#| fig-cap: "Observed ECV and OLS fitted line (ecv_median_cm3 ~ age). Points colored by grade."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

pred = pd.DataFrame({'age_mid_Ma': np.linspace(ecv['age_mid_Ma'].min(),
                                                ecv['age_mid_Ma'].max(), 200)})
pred['ecv_pred'] = model1.predict(pred)

(
    ggplot(ecv, aes(x='age_mid_Ma', y='ecv_median_cm3', color='grade', size='n_estimates'))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.6)
    + geom_line(aes(x='age_mid_Ma', y='ecv_pred'), data=pred,
                color='black', size=1, inherit_aes=False)
    #+ geom_smooth(method='lm', color='blue', linetype='dashed')
    + scale_x_reverse()
    + labs(x='Age (Ma)', y='ECV (cc)', color='Grade',
           title='Hominin ECV through time')
    + theme_bw()
)
```

### 4.2 Inline Python results

The simple regression explains `{python} round(model1.rsquared, 3)` of the variance in ECV. For every additional million years into the past, ECV decreases by `{python} abs(round(model1.params['age_mid_Ma'], 1))` cc on average (p = `{python} round(model1.pvalues['age_mid_Ma'], 4)`).

### 4.3 A model comparison table

Create a summary table comparing the three models from Part 3:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of three OLS models for ECV"

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    'Model': ['ecv_median_cm3 ~ age', 'ecv_median_cm3 ~ age + C(grade)', 'ecv_median_cm3 ~ age * C(grade)'],
    'R-squared': [round(m.rsquared, 3) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
    'Adj. R-squared': [round(m.rsquared_adj, 3) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
    'AIC': [round(m.aic, 1) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
    'N': [int(m.nobs) for m in [model1, model2, model3]]
})
comparison
```
